$comment: Rules for recognising when an attacker is checking whether the box is
real. Data, not code: adding a rule is an edit to this file and a deploy,
Every pattern below was derived from the captured corpus and the counts
are what it actually matched when the rule was written. They are recorded
so a later reader can tell a rule that stopped matching from a rule that
`weight` is deliberate. Reading /proc/cpuinfo is both routine recon and a
core-count check, so it cannot be treated as proof of anything; looking
for a hypervisor by name has no innocent reading. A score keeps the
ambiguity visible instead of forcing a yes/no on evidence that does not
Patterns are matched case-insensitively with word boundaries where the
token is a word. An early draft matched 'kvm' as a bare substring and hit

rules.why: Names the thing directly. Alphanumeric boundaries rather than \b, because \b treats underscore as a word character and would miss test_honeypot_check, which is a real captured command.
Looking for a specific hypervisor. Alphanumeric boundaries: an unbounded 'kvm' matched the password 3HKvmnWk, and \b would still miss a match adjacent to an underscore.
Tools whose only purpose is identifying the platform.
Firmware identity strings give the hypervisor away.
Establishing what the shell can actually do before committing a payload. A real box is assumed to have these; a fake one often claims to.
Testing whether a directory is genuinely writable. Emulated shells commonly report success and write nothing.
Echoing a nonce and checking it comes back is the cheapest test that a shell is real.
Both ordinary recon and a core-count check. Weight 1: suggestive only, never decisive on its own.
Same ambiguity as cpuinfo. Present in almost every botnet's opening sequence.
A freshly booted box with minutes of uptime is a plausible sandbox tell.
Small RAM suggests a sandbox. Also ordinary recon.
Looking for analysis tooling, or for an implausibly empty process table.
An overlay or tmpfs root is a container or a sandbox.
